tldr: This paper represents robot actions as continuous latent functions rather than discrete command sequences, pretraining shared dynamics from diverse robot embodiments and sampling frequencies before connecting them to a world model. The proposed method demonstrates that a single predicted latent function can generate smooth, energy-efficient actions at any chosen control frequency.
hero_caption: Overall architecture and inference flow of CoAWM. In Stage A, a shared action function space is pretrained on heterogeneous robot trajectories across multiple frequencies. In Stage B, it connects to a world-model backbone. During inference, predicting the latent function once from current observations lets users generate end-effector commands for any control frequency simply by querying different time steps.
overview:
When trying to make robots smarter by sharing data across platforms, the biggest hurdle is the divergence in embodiments and control frequencies. Even for a common reach motion, different robots use distinct command interfaces and transmission rates, meaning identical time-series indices correspond to completely different physical timestamps. Conventional world models and policy learning frameworks have struggled to broadly leverage diverse robot datasets due to this mismatch.

To overcome this, the authors introduced a breakthrough: modeling robot actions not as discrete command sequences, but as continuous functions (latent functions) that describe how actions evolve across physical space and time. This approach is realized as Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM). CoAWM learns in two stages. First, in Stage A, it pretrains a shared latent function space via autoencoding on trajectory data collected from various robots and sampling frequencies, enforcing consistency across different temporal sampling views. Next, in Stage B, this pretrained function space connects to a visual world model (LaWAM), conditioning the prediction of latent action functions on camera images, language instructions, and proprioceptive robot states.

Empirical evaluations show that this latent function space reconstructs original action trajectories with extreme precision (2.5 mm in position error and around 0.23 degrees in rotation error). Furthermore, across 16 real dual-arm manipulation tasks, it dramatically reduces initial action jerk compared to a conventional world model (LaWAM)—by 36.7% in position and 54.2% in rotation—delivering substantially smoother motion while matching movement speed. The authors also demonstrate that a single latent function stably executes tasks across a wide frequency range of 10 to 60 Hz and reduces energy consumption by 22.6%.
contributions: Represented robot actions as continuous latent action functions rather than discrete command sequences, building a shared representation space that can be queried at arbitrary frequencies.
Proposed a self-supervised pretraining framework that extracts shared spatiotemporal dynamics priors from trajectory data across diverse embodiments and sampling frequencies.

Introduced a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture and geometric anchoring for unified processing of translation, rotation, and gripper states, balancing physical continuity with high reconstruction fidelity.
Connected a visual world model to the latent function space, maintaining high task success rates across varying execution frequencies while reducing initial jerk and lowering energy consumption.

sections.heading: How can we unify mismatched control frequencies and robot embodiments?
sections.summary: While the demand for sharing experiences across different robots is growing, mismatched control frequencies and command formats pose serious challenges. By treating motions as continuous functions, this paper proposes CoAWM to pretrain shared dynamics from heterogeneous robot trajectories and connect them to a world model.
sections.details:
In robotics, transferring data collected on one robot to another (cross-embodiment learning) has long been a dream. However, changing the robot changes the control frequency, so identical array indices correspond to entirely different physical times. Simply standardizing the storage format does not solve this fundamental problem.

The core insight here is a paradigm shift: move away from sampled command sequences as the basic unit, and instead learn the spatiotemporal evolution of actions directly as a latent function. Once actions are represented as a function, querying it at any physical timestamp extracts control commands at whatever frequency is needed.

This cleanly separates the problem into two parts: first, learning spatiotemporal dynamics priors from diverse robot trajectories, and second, selecting the appropriate action function conditioned on the current scene and instruction. CoAWM realizes this via a two-stage learning pipeline, enabling broad data utilization and flexible execution frequencies.

Note how decoupling actions as functions simultaneously enables diverse pretraining sources and runtime frequency flexibility.

sections.heading: At the intersection of continuous actions, cross-embodiment learning, and world models
sections.summary: This section reviews conventional action chunking, diffusion policies, and movement primitives like DMPs to contextualize the work. It also surveys recent large-scale cross-embodiment learning and world-model literature, explaining how CoAWM unifies them.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Continuous Action and Functional Representations
Robot action representations have seen diverse developments, from action chunking in ACT and sequence generation with Diffusion Policy to frequency tokenization in FAST. Meanwhile, continuous formulations aware of physical time have a long history, including Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) and probabilistic movement primitives (ProDMPs) based on dynamical systems. More recently, efforts have explored functionalizing actions using B-splines and neural implicit representations (Implicit Action Fields). CoAWM builds on the advantages of these functional representations, elevating them into a framework that extracts shared dynamics from heterogeneous robot data.

### 2.2 Cross-Embodiment Learning and Action Priors
Efforts to channel diverse robot datasets into a single foundation model are advancing rapidly, as seen in Open X-Embodiment, Octo, and π0. A central challenge is disentangling robot-specific command spaces from cross-robot sharable action knowledge. Prior works like LAPA, UniVLA, and LAC-WM learn latent actions from video, but CoAWM stands out by learning action trajectories directly through a latent function autoencoder, naturally accommodating variations in sampling frequency.

### 2.3 World Models for Action Generation and Execution
World models support action selection through future prediction. Works such as V-JEPA 2, LaWAM, and AHA-WAM have emerged, with LaWAM specifically tackling physical time alignment and mixed-frequency training. By preserving the strong visual predictive capabilities of world models while interfacing the output with a continuous latent function space, CoAWM yields an architecture remarkably resilient to runtime latency and frequency shifts.

sections.heading: Pretraining latent action functions and connecting them to world models
sections.summary: This section details the CoAWM methodology. In Stage A, an MoT encoder pretrains latent functions from multi-frequency, heterogeneous robot trajectories. In Stage B, these are coupled with a world model that takes visual tokens, language, and proprioception to generate actions.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Overview
CoAWM represents action rollouts as a latent function $Z$ over physical time. Training proceeds in two stages: Stage A pretrains an encoder $E_\phi$ and decoder $D_\psi$ on time-stamped trajectory data, and Stage B connects them to a world-model backbone to predict an environment-conditioned latent function $\hat{Z}$.

### 3.2 Continuous Action Function Representation
An action trajectory is defined as a tuple of timestamps, end-effector commands, and valid masks: $\mathcal{A}=\{(\tau_i, a_i, m_i)\}_{i=1}^N$. The current time is defined as physical time $\tau=0$, spanning an execution horizon of 1.2 seconds.
- **Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) Encoder**: Translation (XYZ), quaternion rotation (Q), and gripper (G) streams are processed with distinct expert parameters while sharing attention across all streams. This preserves modality-specific features while capturing temporal coordination, compressing the trajectory into a latent function $Z$ of 96 tokens total (32 tokens per modality, width 256).
- **Independent Temporal Queries**: The decoder takes requested physical times $\tau$, Fourier features, modality embeddings, and execution context, cross-attending into the latent memory to read out actions. Because each temporal query is evaluated independently, it does not depend on the number or order of time points, allowing decoding at arbitrary frequencies.
- **Geometric Anchoring**: To ensure smooth predictions, positions are reconstructed as offsets relative to the initial state $p_0$ via $p(\tau) = p_0 + \widetilde{p}(\tau)$, and rotations are expressed through quaternion multiplication with the initial rotation $q_0$ via $q(\tau) = r(\tau) \otimes q_0$. This strictly recovers the current state at $\tau=0$. For the gripper's discrete transitions, nearest-neighbor lookup over time-indexed knot points is used.

### 3.3 Learning Heterogeneous Embodiment Dynamics Priors (Stage A)
Two views $\mathcal{A}^{(1)}$ and $\mathcal{A}^{(2)}$ at different sampling frequencies are created from the same physical motion. Passing both through the shared encoder yields latent variables $Z^{(1)}$ and $Z^{(2)}$. Reconstruction losses (translation error, geodesic angular rotation error, gripper error) are enforced on both original points and a shared 60 Hz (73-point) query grid, paired with an MSE loss between latents for consistency. Because this requires neither images nor language, it scales efficiently on raw trajectory logs.

### 3.4 World-Model Interfacing (Stage B)
The pretrained function space connects to the LaWAM backbone. VLM features, predicted future visual tokens, and robot proprioception are combined into cross-attention memory, adding current visual tokens as a residual to predict the latent function $\hat{Z}$. Training supervises this head using cosine similarity against expert latents from the frozen action encoder, alongside reconstruction loss on decoded actions.

### 3.5 Action Execution via Temporal Querying
During inference, the latent function is predicted once per replanning cycle (1.2 seconds). Control loops can then run smoothly at high speed simply by feeding time queries corresponding to the desired frequency $f$ (e.g., $1.2 \times 30 = 36$ steps for 30 Hz) into the decoder.

sections.heading: High fidelity, superior initial smoothness, and flexible execution frequencies
sections.summary: CoAWM is evaluated across trajectory representation fidelity, closed-loop task performance, cross-frequency execution, and motion quality (jerk and energy). It reduces jerk by up to 54% compared to LaWAM and executes tasks stably from 10 to 60 Hz.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Continuous Action Representation Fidelity
Reconstruction error for the pretrained function autoencoder was measured across a held-out set of 8,192 action windows. It achieved high accuracy, yielding a translation error of just 2.503 mm and a rotation error of 0.2295 degrees. This demonstrates that the latent function space preserves fine-grained trajectory details with minimal loss.

### 4.2 Dramatic Initial Execution Smoothing Without Sacrificing Speed
Motion quality during the first second of execution was compared against the baseline (LaWAM) across 16 tasks and 800 paired trials under identical initial conditions.
- **Translation Jerk (Jerk RMS)**: Decreased by 36.7%, from 150.87 to 95.46.
- **Rotation Jerk (Jerk RMS)**: Decreased by 54.2%, from 746.06 to 341.73.
- **Average Velocity (Velocity RMS)**: Remained essentially identical at 0.332 for the proposed method versus 0.338 for LaWAM.
Rather than artificially slowing down movements, the approach eliminates abrupt acceleration spikes (chatter) while sustaining motion speed. Overall task success reached 75.1%.

### 4.3 Multitask Dual-Arm Manipulation Across Frequencies
On dual-arm manipulation tasks (including Bottle, A2B, Burger, and Hammer), the method achieved high success rates between 86% and 94% across 50 trials each. Furthermore, testing across query frequencies of 10, 15, 20, 30, 50, and 60 Hz over 150 trials each (maintaining the 1.2-second window) yielded 116, 121, 117, 119, 116, and 110 successes respectively, demonstrating robust task execution regardless of frequency.

### 4.4 Reduced Execution Energy Consumption
Evaluating positive mechanical work estimated via PD torques across 13 scenarios where both methods succeeded revealed a 22.6% reduction in mean work, dropping from 506.66 to 392.13 (improving in 12 out of 13 scenarios). This quantitatively verifies that smoother actions reduce unnecessary stress on the robot's motors.

sections.heading: A new benchmark for action quality and prospects for scaling
sections.summary: This section discusses the value of separating action structure learning from the choice of execution frequency. It highlights the establishment of smoothness and energy efficiency as evaluation metrics alongside success rate, while considering future challenges for full fine-tuning on larger datasets.
sections.details:
The primary triumph of this research lies in completely decoupling the learning of physical action progression from the runtime control frequency. This allows the same model to adapt seamlessly from low-bandwidth communication environments to responsive, high-speed control loops.

Moreover, while prior imitation learning and world-model literature often focused exclusively on task success rate, this paper brings motion quality itself—such as motion smoothness (jerk reduction) and energy consumption (mechanical work)—to the forefront as key evaluation axes. Mitigating hardware wear and thermal buildup caused by jerky motions is critical when operating real physical robots.

At the same time, challenges remain. While initial execution is remarkably smooth, continuous long-horizon execution and frequent replanning still exhibit lingering jerk effects (jerk tails). The authors plan to address long-term execution stability by incorporating more diverse robot embodiments and sampling rates into pretraining, coupled with end-to-end full fine-tuning of the entire world model.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Physical-time functional representations unlock new frontiers in robot learning
sections.summary: CoAWM integrates action representation learning, world-model prediction, and temporal query execution through a shared function space. Early experiments confirm high reconstruction fidelity, dual-arm proficiency, and substantial gains in motion quality, establishing a solid foundation for future scaling.
sections.details:
CoAWM introduces a framework that pairs spatiotemporal dynamics pretrained on heterogeneous robot trajectories with the contextual understanding of visual world models.

By formulating actions as continuous functions, it surmounts the barrier of mismatched control clocks across robots, outlining a clear path toward scaling diverse data sources into a single model. Initial dual-arm validation experiments demonstrate high-precision trajectory recovery, multitask success, significant jerk reduction, and improved energy efficiency. This marks an important milestone toward generalist robot foundation models that operate safely and flexibly in the physical world.

takeaways: Representing robot actions as latent functions over physical time rather than discrete steps enables data integration and action execution independent of control frequencies.
Decoupling action pretraining (Stage A) from task-conditioned world-model interfacing (Stage B) allows effective use of vast robot trajectory logs lacking visual or language annotations.
Combining continuous function representations with geometric anchoring reduces initial jerk by over 30% to 50% and cuts energy consumption by more than 20% without sacrificing execution speed.
limitations: While the initial one-second execution window is exceptionally smooth, lingering jerk artifacts (jerk tails) remain during long-horizon rollouts and at replanning boundaries.
The current study is positioned as a rapid validation, leaving full fine-tuning across large-scale, multi-robot datasets for future investigation.
Handling discontinuous, discrete behaviors like gripper opening and closing requires a heuristic nearest-neighbor lookup over time knots rather than a purely continuous function.
